```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.2,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

Panel data (also called longitudinal data, repeated measures or
time-series cross-section) records the same individuals over time: employees over
weeks, patients over visits, firms over years, regions over quarters. The rows are
long — one row per individual and time point — and the analysis usually involves
two questions at once: what happened over time within each individual, and how do
individuals compare once they are grouped.

**panelviz** turns one declaration of *which column is the individual* and *which
column is time* into aggregated tables and publication-ready charts. This vignette
walks through the whole workflow on a simulated dataset, so it runs without any
downloads.

## Declare the panel

We simulate 120 employees observed weekly for half a year, with some weeks
missing so the panel is unbalanced — the common case in practice.

```{r data}
library(panelviz)

set.seed(42)
people <- data.frame(
  person = sprintf("p%03d", 1:120),
  team = sample(
    c("Sales", "Operations", "Finance", "Support", "Technology"),
    120, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.30, 0.25, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15)
  )
)
grid <- expand.grid(
  person = people$person,
  week = 0:25,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
grid$week <- as.Date("2024-01-01") + grid$week * 7

d <- merge(grid, people, by = "person")
d <- d[stats::runif(nrow(d)) > 0.08, ]           # drop some weeks: unbalanced
d$score <- 55 +
  as.numeric(factor(d$team)) * 2 +               # teams differ in level
  0.2 * as.numeric(d$week - as.Date("2024-01-01")) / 7 +  # slow upward trend
  stats::rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 5)                    # individual noise
```

`as_panel()` declares the individual and the time column. It recognises the time
format, sorts the data and reports the shape of the panel:

```{r declare}
panel <- as_panel(d, id = person, time = week, source = "Simulated data")
panel
```

The header tells you how many individuals and periods there are, whether the
panel is balanced, and how many rows were read. The `source` given here is
printed in the footer of every chart drawn from the panel.

## Time formats are detected

Dates, years, quarters (`"1998 Q1"`), months (`"2020-03"`), ISO weeks, hourly
timestamps, Stata `%tm` and `%tq` values and plain indices are all recognised.
`panel_meta()` reports what was detected:

```{r meta}
panel_meta(panel)[c("id", "time", "kind", "freq", "n_ids", "n_periods", "balanced")]
```

Ambiguous input stops with an informative error rather than being guessed; pass
`time_format` (a `strptime()` string such as `"%d.%m.%Y"`, or a name such as
`"year"`) when you know the format.

## Aggregate in two stages

A panel has two dimensions, so aggregation happens in two stages. First, time is
collapsed *within* each individual (`fun_time`), then individuals are collapsed
into groups (`fun_group`):

```{r aggregate}
head(
  panel_aggregate(panel, "score",
                  by = "team", period = "week",
                  fun_time = "mean", fun_group = "mean"),
  8
)
```

The `.n` column is the number of individuals behind each value. Use `fun_time = "sum"`
for flows and `"last"` for stocks or cumulative counts, `fun_group = "median"` or
`"p90"` for other summaries, and `min_n` to suppress groups with too few
individuals (the chart footer reports the suppression).

## Charts

Every chart function takes the same arguments: `by` (grouping column), `period`,
`fun_time`, `fun_group`, `min_n`, `tag`, `source`, `style` and `return`.

### Lines

One overall series, or one line per group with direct labels at the last observed
value. Titles are computed from the data:

```{r line}
panel_line(panel, "score")
```

```{r line-by}
panel_line(panel, "score", by = "team")
```

Coarsen time with `period`, add a privacy floor with `min_n`, or highlight one
group and index every group to 100 at its first period:

```{r line-coarsen}
panel_line(panel, "score", by = "team", period = "month", min_n = 25)
```

```{r line-highlight}
panel_line(panel, "score", by = "team", highlight = "Technology", index = TRUE)
```

### Heatmap

Groups (rows) by time (columns), sorted by level:

```{r heatmap}
panel_heatmap(panel, "score", by = "team", period = "week")
```

### Band

The median line with a shaded percentile band shows the spread across
individuals, not just the centre:

```{r band}
panel_band(panel, "score", by = "team", lower = "p10", upper = "p90")
```

### Bars

Time is collapsed (`period = "all"` by default) and groups are ranked:

```{r bar}
panel_bar(panel, "score", by = "team", fun_group = "median")
```

### Distribution

Each individual's average over time, then the distribution across individuals:

```{r distribution}
panel_distribution(panel, "score", by = "team")
```

### Spaghetti

Thin lines for a random sample of individuals with the group average on top:

```{r spaghetti}
panel_spaghetti(panel, "score", n_ids = 40, seed = 1)
```

## Get the numbers behind a chart

Every chart takes `return = "table"` and returns exactly what it drew — a tibble
with the aggregated values, the period, the number of individuals and the group:

```{r table}
head(panel_line(panel, "score", by = "team", return = "table"), 8)
```

## Styles, tags and overrides

Five looks ship with the package, and any computed text can be overridden:

```{r styles}
panel_styles()
```

```{r style-tag}
panel_line(
  panel, "score", by = "team",
  style = "ft", tag = 1,
  title = "Scores rose across every team",
  source = "Simulated data"
)
```

`use_panel_style("dark")` sets the default for the whole session.

## Numbered multi-panel figures

`panel_figure()` lays several charts out under one headline, numbers the panels
and shares one source and notes footer:

```{r figure, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5}
panel_figure(
  list(
    panel_line(panel, "score", by = "team"),
    panel_heatmap(panel, "score", by = "team"),
    panel_bar(panel, "score", by = "team", fun_group = "median"),
    panel_distribution(panel, "score", by = "team")
  ),
  title = "Four views of one panel",
  subtitle = "Weekly scores by team, 120 simulated employees",
  source = "Simulated data",
  notes = "Individuals are simulated employees."
)
```

Save any chart or figure with `save_panel(fig, "figure.png", width = 12, height = 8)`.

## Reading real data

`read_panel()` declares a file or URL as a panel — csv, tsv, Stata, SPSS and rds
are supported, and Stata variable labels become chart names:

```{r read, eval = FALSE}
nls <- read_panel("nlswork.dta", id = idcode, time = year)
gm  <- read_panel("gapminder.csv", id = country, time = year)

# composite individual: several columns
tour <- read_panel("tourism.csv", id = c(Region, State, Purpose), time = Quarter)
```

Wide data (one column per period) is pivoted to long format first:

```{r wide, eval = FALSE}
as_panel_wide(wide, id = company, cols = starts_with("inc"))
```

- `panel_styles()` lists the five looks; `save_panel()` writes PNG, PDF or
  PostScript at a chosen size.
- The README has a longer gallery of examples, including tracking charts,
  stacked bars and small multiples.
